hardWords.accolade: The blow with the flat of a sword that makes a man a knight; later, any public honor.
hardWords.hauberk: A shirt of mail, reaching at least to the knees.
hardWords.mail: Armor of interlinked iron rings (from French maille, “mesh”).
hardWords.visor: The grated or slotted face-piece of a helmet, raised or lowered in a groove.
hardWords.bever: A helmet piece that could be opened so the wearer might drink (from Italian bevere).
hardWords.ventayle: The air-passage of a helmet; another name for the bever.
hardWords.esquire: The rank between page and knight; a youth in training, usually from about fourteen.
hardWords.page: A boy, often from age seven, serving in a castle while he learns courtesy and arms.
hardWords.errant: Wandering; a knight-errant rides in quest of adventure and redress of wrongs.
hardWords.joust: A combat of two knights with lances, aiming to unhorse one another; narrower than a tournament.
hardWords.tournament: A larger martial pageant of many knights, meant to show skill as well as force.
hardWords.sangreal: The Holy Grail; in these romances, the vessel of the Last Supper.
hardWords.paynim: A pagan, in medieval Christian usage; often a Saracen in the romances.
hardWords.guerdon: A reward, especially one given by a lady to her knight.
hardWords.favor: A token of a lady’s regard—scarf, sleeve, or veil—worn on a knight’s helm or shield.
hardWords.lists: The fenced ground of a tournament.
hardWords.curtesie: Courtesy; the manners of a court.
hardWords.wharfs: The landing-places of a river town; here, Camelot’s shore.
hardWords.escalibore: Excalibur, Arthur’s sword; Bulfinch also writes Excalibar.
hardWords.paynyms: Pagans (Caxton’s spelling in the Morte d’Arthur).
hardWords.troubadours: Poets of the south of France (langue d’oc) who sang of love and satire.
hardWords.trouveurs: Poets of northern France (langue d’oïl) who told adventure-romances.
hardWords.langue d'oc: The southern French speech in which “yes” was oc.
hardWords.langue d'oil: The northern French speech in which “yes” was oïl (later oui).
hardWords.varlet: A young attendant; another word for a page.
hardWords.villain: Here a bonded peasant (villein), not “scoundrel”; attached to the soil.
hardWords.serf: A slave of the lowest kind, whose labor belonged wholly to a lord.
hardWords.clerk: Anyone in clerical orders—or, later, anyone who could read, and so claim “benefit of clergy.”
hardWords.benefit of clergy: Exemption, for those counted clerks, from some capital punishments.
hardWords.plate: Solid iron pieces shaped to the body; later armor, after about 1300.
hardWords.doublet: A padded garment worn under mail to take the shock of a blow.
hardWords.spurs: The last tokens given in the making of a knight; “to win one’s spurs.”
hardWords.Camelot: Arthur’s chief court in the later romances.
hardWords.Avalon: The island to which Arthur is borne after Camlann, to be healed—or to wait.
hardWords.Modred: Arthur’s treacherous kinsman; also spelled Mordred.
hardWords.Igraine: Arthur’s mother; wife first of Gorlois, then of Uther.
hardWords.Nimue: A Lady of the Lake; in some tellings she imprisons Merlin.
hardWords.Viviane: Another name of the damsel who beguiles Merlin.
hardWords.Enid: Geraint’s wife, type of patience and truth.
hardWords.Olwen: The maiden whose hair is yellow as broom; Kilwich’s destined wife.
hardWords.Elphin: The luckless prince who finds the infant Taliesin in a weir.
hardWords.weir: A fish-trap built in a river.
hardWords.boon: A favor asked of a king or a knight, which honor then requires him to grant.
hardWords.quest: A search undertaken as a point of honor, especially the Grail quest.
hardWords.Round Table: Arthur’s table, made so that no knight should claim a higher seat than another.

arthur-i:0.source: Robert de Beauvais, quoted by Scott
arthur-i:0.note: Bulfinch gives a scrap of thirteenth-century French so you can hear the language of the Norman court. The ‘matter’ (matyere) is Tristram’s story, already so often told that the poet will not ‘say too much.’

allusions.note: The same hero as Tristram; the spelling shows how the name moved from French into English.
Scott printed early romances and used them in his own poems; Bulfinch borrows the specimen from Scott’s introduction to Sir Tristrem.

arthur-i:1.note: This is English of the common people after the Conquest. ‘Strange Inglis’ means the Frenchified speech of the nobility, not a foreign language in our sense.

allusions.note: English. Brunne writes for ‘simple men’ who cannot follow court French.

arthur-i:2.source: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte Darthur (1485), in Caxton’s spelling
arthur-i:2.note: Malory’s ‘nine worthies’ are a medieval hall of fame: three pagans, three Jews, three Christians. Arthur is placed with Charlemagne and Godfrey of Bouillon. Read a few lines aloud; the spelling is less wild if you sound it.

allusions.note: The Nine Worthies, a standard late-medieval list of exemplary captains.
Godfrey of Bouillon, a leader of the First Crusade and first ruler of Jerusalem.

arthur-ii:0.note: This chapter follows Milton’s History of Britain as well as Geoffrey of Monmouth. The poems here are literary ornaments: they show how later English poets treated Brutus, Lear, and Arthur as if they were history.

allusions.note: An old name of Britain; in the myth, a giant son of Neptune.
Not the Roman; a Trojan great-grandson of Aeneas, invented to give Britain a classical pedigree.

arthur-iii:0.source: Spenser, The Faerie Queene, and later verse on Merlin
arthur-iii:0.note: Merlin is less a stage magician here than a prophet-engineer: he moves stones, hides a king, and is at last trapped by his own craft. Spenser’s stanzas make the cave a moral landscape—listen for the hollow sound.

allusions.note: The damsel of the Lake who learns Merlin’s art and imprisons him; names vary by romance.
Geoffrey has Merlin fetch the stones from Ireland; the ‘Giant’s Dance’ is an older name for the circle.

arthur-iv:0.source: Verse on Arthur’s crowning and Excalibur
arthur-iv:0.note: Watch the two swords: the sword in the stone proves the king; the sword from the Lake (Excalibur) is a gift that must later be returned. Poets like the second better, because it can be thrown back.

allusions.note: Excalibur. ‘Hight’ means ‘is called.’
Not Tennyson’s Elaine of Astolat; an older water-spirit who fosters Lancelot and arms Arthur.

arthur-vi:0.source: Ballad of Gawain and the Green Knight / related romance verse
arthur-vi:0.note: Gawain’s courtesy is the point. A challenge that looks like mere strength is really a test of truth-telling. If a line feels abrupt, it is the ballad’s way: action, then speech, then action.

allusions.note: A supernatural challenger; in the great Middle English poem he is bound to Morgan le Fay and to a Christmas game.

arthur-vii:1.source: The Boy and the Mantle (traditional ballad)
arthur-vii:1.note: A ‘mantle test’ is a folk motif: a magic garment fits only the faithful wife. Guenever fails; Cradock’s lady almost fails, then confesses a kiss and is cleared. Read it as court satire, not as a sermon. Hard words sit in the clothing: kirtle, ouches, curtesie.

allusions.note: A northern Arthurian court in many ballads, instead of Camelot.
The same knight as Caradoc Briefbras in the prose tale just above.

arthur-x:0.source: Alfred, Lord Tennyson, The Lady of Shalott
arthur-x:0.note: Tennyson retells Elaine of Astolat as a weaver who may not look at Camelot except in a mirror. When she looks at Lancelot, the curse holds: she dies on the river. ‘Corse’ is corpse. Notice that Lancelot’s only speech is courteous and late—too late, which is the poem’s sting.

allusions.note: The same place; Malory’s Elaine of Astolat becomes Tennyson’s Lady of Shalott.
Here a town of towers and wharfs, seen from outside—the Lady never belongs to it.

arthur-xii:0.note: The love-potion is not a modern ‘excuse’; in the romance it is a fate the lovers drink and then must live. Songs in this chapter often belong to Iseult’s grief or to Tristram’s harp.

allusions.note: The same queen; Irish in origin, married to King Mark of Cornwall.
Tristram’s uncle and liege; the tragedy is that love and loyalty cannot both be kept.

arthur-xiii:0.note: When a dying or exiled knight ‘sings,’ the poem is doing the work of an inner speech. Look for the proper names: they tell you which court he has lost.

allusions.note: Tristram’s other home; there is often a second Iseult (‘of the White Hands’) in that land.

arthur-xv:0.note: The Table is a political image: equality among peers under one king. Poets like it because a circle has no ‘head of the table’ except the king’s presence.

allusions.note: A seat. The Siege Perilous is the vacant place reserved for the Grail knight.

arthur-xviii:0.note: Perceval’s fault is often silence: he does not ask whom the Grail serves. In poetry that withheld question becomes a moral: courtesy without charity is incomplete.

allusions.note: The wounded keeper of the Grail castle; the land fails with him.

arthur-xix:0.source: Grail poetry (including later English verse Bulfinch quotes)
arthur-xix:0.note: Sangreal is ‘Holy Grail.’ The romances never quite agree whether it is a cup, a dish, or a vision. What they agree on: only the pure see it plainly.

allusions.note: In Grail legend he brings the vessel to Britain.
Lancelot’s son, begotten in enchantment; the knight who succeeds where his father cannot.

arthur-xxiii:0.source: Morte d’Arthur verse; Wordsworth and others on Arthur’s return
arthur-xxiii:0.note: ‘Morte’ means death, but the tradition refuses to let Arthur stay dead. The barge to Avalon, the returned sword, the once and future king: keep those three images distinct as you read.

allusions.note: The apple-island of healing; in some tellings Arthur sleeps there until Britain’s need.
The last knight, charged to throw Excalibur back to the water—and tempted to keep it.

mabinogi-xiii:0.note: Taliesin speaks as a child and as a seer at once. Welsh bardic poems in translation keep the short line and the boast: small as I am, I shall be more than three hundred salmon.

allusions.note: A fish-trap that should have made Elphin rich; it yields a poet instead.
The prince whose luck turns when he takes up the child.

hero-robin:0.note: The refrain ‘God save Robin Hood and all his good yeomanry’ is the people’s blessing. Yeoman here is a free fighting man, not a knight—an important contrast after so many chapters of the Round Table.

allusions.note: The setting many later tellings choose; the earliest ballads are less exact about kings.
